summary: Automated tools struggle primarily in three structural microdrama scenarios where screenplay text departs from visual/narrative nuance.

failure_categories.explanation: Scenes with minimal dialogue but high visual tension (e.g., intense 5-second eye contact or a physical comedic gesture) receive lower text-heuristic scores despite being great video clips.
failure_categories.example: Episode 12: A scene consisting mostly of silent stares between guards and Juliana is under-ranked because text parser sees low word count.

failure_categories.explanation: Clips with intense shouting about past lineage, obscure family names, or deep legal contracts score high on emotion keywords but fail the 'Standalone' test for a cold viewer on TikTok who has never watched the series.
failure_categories.example: Episode 34: Characters arguing passionately about inheritance bylaws scores 9.2 on emotion but confuses a first-time viewer without prior 30 episodes context.

failure_categories.explanation: Slow-burn psychological manipulation scenes get cut mid-build because the heuristic looks for immediate explosive words in the first 3 seconds.
failure_categories.example: Episode 21: A quiet, chilling whisper dialogue gets deprioritized over a louder but less sophisticated shouting match.

mitigation_strategy: 1. Add visual frame analysis (multimodal video model) when video renders exist. 2. Human editor in the loop for final pass/approval via the Streamlit review dashboard.
